note: Main line: Checkpoint Seven (military). Every scene is data. main_line scenes have weight 0 and play in act order; the raid rolls them onto a green-marked node so the player walks to the story instead of being ambushed by it. Attribute points are scarce: one delta per act at most, never in a repeatable scene.

events.title: STOPPED
events.text: A hand takes your collar and puts you against the wall. No shouting. Boots apart, hands flat, and a voice at your ear: 'North side. How many were there.' He means soldiers, not people. The muzzle stays where it is until you answer.

outcome.log: He steps back and lets you breathe. 'Seven. Checkpoint seven. Bring diesel.' He gives you a torn strip of paper with the grid on it.
He writes it down. 'Then we hold longer than they do.' He lets you go without telling you where to find them.
You get an elbow in the ribs and a rifle butt across the shoulder. He takes your medkit and walks off. The checkpoint heard about you either way.

events.title: TWO CANS
events.text: Checkpoint seven is three concrete blocks and a tin roof. A corporal is counting magazines, a medic is unwrapping the same bandage for the third time. Nobody asks where the fuel came from. 'Can you do two more?' the corporal says. 'That is the whole question.'

outcome.log: They pour one in and keep one in the shade. The corporal writes your name on a scrap of the duty sheet, which is the closest they have to a promise.

choices.label: ONE CAN. THE OTHER IS MINE.

outcome.log: The medic notes it, small and exact, the way medics note things. Nobody argues with you.
The corporal empties his pockets into your hand without a word and turns back to the magazines.

events.title: THE RADIO
events.text: Their set is old, military, and dead without a rechargeable cell. The corporal sketches it on the back of the duty sheet: old station, second floor, third locker, pry it. In the locker, under the cell, there is a stack of letters that were never posted. Same addressee on all of them, same handwriting.

outcome.log: The set comes up that night. All it brings back is a carrier tone and a callsign, repeating.
The corporal reads one, folds it, puts it in his breast pocket and does not mention it again. The medic looks at the floor.
The lieutenant did not go south to desert. He went south to ask why the relief never came. The letter says so in his own hand.

events.title: THE LIEUTENANT
events.text: He is in the drainage ditch behind the motor pool, buttons done up, no weapon on him, a wax-sealed dispatch case under his arm. The case holds one sheet: a list of numbers, a date, and a printed line - 'the above will be withdrawn; all others hold in place'.

choices.label: TAKE THE CASE BACK TO THEM

outcome.log: The corporal breaks the seal himself, in front of you, and reads it twice before he says anything.

choices.label: TAKE HIM BACK. LEAVE THE CASE.

outcome.log: They carry him in on a door panel. Nobody asks what was in the case, and that is the point.

choices.label: BURN THE SHEET. KEEP THE CASE.

outcome.log: Wax and paper go up together behind the motor pool. What they do not know cannot be taken from them.

events.title: HOLD IN PLACE
events.text: The corporal has the sheet. He has read it. He asks it quietly, with the torch off: 'Are any of our three numbers on this list.' The medic is counting magazines again, out loud, from the beginning.

outcome.log: He nods once and goes to wake the medic. They start filling sandbags at the north face of the checkpoint. Nobody asks you to stay.
He folds the sheet and puts it in his pocket. 'Then we hold,' he says, 'and you should not be here when it starts.'

choices.label: GIVE THEM THE CASE AND THE NUMBERS

outcome.log: You put the case on the crate and read the three numbers out loud yourself. Better a voice they know.

choices.label: LEAVE THE SHEET AND WALK AWAY

outcome.log: You hear the first shot before you reach the fence. Whether it was theirs or for them, you will not find out tonight.

events.title: A MAN IN THE STAIRWELL
events.text: He is bleeding against the wall between floors, holding his side together with a hand that has stopped being useful. He has a pistol and no boots, and he looks at you the way you look at weather.

outcome.log: He lives. He leaves you his pistol, which is not worth much, and a name you will hear again.
He does not argue. The stairwell is quiet afterwards.
You take the stairs two at a time. Behind you, nothing, and then nothing.
